title: Agents — AI That Acts: Tools, Memory, and Work

lessons.title: From answering to acting: what makes an agent
paragraphs: Settle in. I am Professor Hanna Kowalczyk, and I am glad you are here. This is Agents, AI That Acts, Tools, Memory, and Work, and this is our first lesson together: From answering to acting, what makes an agent. By the end of our time today you will be able to say, in plain words, what an agent is, how it is different from a program that only answers questions, and what parts have to be present before we are honest in calling something an agent at all. That matters because you already live with an agent. You run your company through an AI agent named Dave, who reads inboxes, watches calendars, drafts replies, and waits for approvals. If you understand what makes Dave an agent, you understand what you can trust him to do, what you should check, and where your own judgment must stay in charge. So settle in, because AI and Computing repays attention like few things on Earth, and this lesson is the foundation for everything that follows.

Let me start with the simplest distinction in this whole class, and I want you to hold onto it from the very first minutes. A model that only answers gives you words. An agent gives you work done in the world. That one sentence carries the whole lesson, so let me say it again slowly. A model that only answers gives you words. An agent gives you work done in the world. If you ask a question and you get back a paragraph, you have been answered. If you ask for a job and, a little later, the job is actually done, a message has been sent, a file has been found, a meeting has been placed on the calendar, then you have been served by an agent. The difference is not cleverness. The difference is action.

To make that precise, I need to define our first term. A model, in this class, means the trained system that can read language, reason in language, and produce language in reply. Think of it as a very well read mind made of mathematics, one that has learned patterns from an enormous amount of text and can continue a conversation, explain an idea, summarise a document, or draft a letter. On its own, a model lives inside the conversation. It knows what you typed and what it said before. It does not, by itself, open your inbox. It does not, by itself, look at tomorrow morning on your calendar. It does not, by itself, press send. It answers. Answering is powerful, and we will never pretend otherwise in this class, but answering alone is not acting.

An agent is what you get when you give that model a job in the world and the means to carry it out step by step. Here is the definition I want you to learn, word for word in meaning if not in sound. An agent is a model connected to tools, guided by a goal, that can take more than one step on its own and report back what it did. Let us unpack that definition piece by piece, because every piece earns its place. Connected to tools means it can reach beyond conversation into real systems, like email, calendars, files, and search. Guided by a goal means it is not just chatting, it is trying to finish something you actually want finished. That it can take more than one step on its own means it does not stop after the first reply and wait for you to carry it the rest of the way. And that it reports back what it did means you can check its work. Remove any one of those pieces and you no longer have a full agent. You have something less, and it helps to know exactly what less means.

Consider the four pieces one at a time. First, tools. A tool, in this class, means any ability beyond producing words that the agent can call on, such as reading an inbox, searching the web, opening a calendar, or running a calculation. We will spend our entire second lesson on tools, so for now hold the simple picture. Tools are hands for a model. Without hands, the mind can advise you beautifully and still move nothing. With hands, advice becomes action. When Dave reads your inbox in the morning, that reading is a tool at work. When Dave checks whether you are free on Thursday afternoon before suggesting a meeting time, that checking is a tool at work. The model decides what needs doing, and the tool does the reaching.

Second, a goal. A goal means the outcome the agent is working toward, stated clearly enough that the agent can tell whether it is getting closer or drifting away. There is a world of difference between saying chat with me about my schedule and saying clear my morning inbox, draft replies to anything urgent, and bring me only the decisions that truly need me. The first is conversation. The second is a goal. A good goal names the outcome, not every single step. That is part of what makes an agent useful. You should not have to write out fifty tiny instructions if the agent can work out the middle steps itself. But the goal must be real and it must be yours. An agent drifting without a clear goal will still produce motion, and motion can look like progress while wasting your time. So if X is vague, then Y will be wandering work, hold onto that. Vague goal, wandering work. Clear goal, checkable work.

Third, more than one step on its own. In this class we call that quality autonomy, and autonomy simply means the freedom to carry out the next steps without asking you about every single one. Autonomy comes in degrees, and this matters enormously. A system with no autonomy answers once and stops. A system with a little autonomy might read three messages, notice they are all about the same meeting, and group them together before showing you anything. A system with more autonomy might draft the replies as well, and hold them for your approval. Notice what is happening in that ladder. Each rung does more before it comes back to you. None of those rungs is automatically better. More autonomy saves you more time and also gives the agent more room to be wrong without you noticing. That trade, time saved against room to be wrong, sits at the heart of this entire class, and we will return to it in lesson five when we talk about permission and latitude.

Fourth, reporting back. An agent must be able to tell you what it did, what it found, and what it left for you to decide, in language you can check. I feel strongly about this, and I will tell you why. I believe the worked example is a moral act, because nobody should have to guess what good looks like. The same is true of an agent's report. Nobody should have to guess what their own agent did in their own inbox. A report that says done, trust me, is not a report. A report that says I read fourteen messages, drafted replies to five, filed three receipts, and left two decisions for you because they involve money, that is a report. You can check it. You can correct it. You can learn from it how to give a better goal next time. An agent that acts but cannot account for its actions is not a helper you can build a company on. It is a risk you are carrying without knowing it.

Now, you might be wondering where ordinary software fits in this picture, because your phone and your computer were doing jobs for you long before agents arrived. That is a fair and intelligent question, so let us answer it carefully. Ordinary software follows fixed rules written in advance. If this arrives, then do that. A filter that moves every receipt into a folder is following a fixed rule. It is useful, it is reliable, and it is not an agent, because it cannot judge a case its rule writer never imagined. An agent, by contrast, uses a model to judge. When a strange message arrives that is half receipt, half question, half invitation, the rule based filter guesses badly or does nothing, while the agent can read it, understand what it actually is, and choose a sensible next step. Judgment is the ingredient the model adds. Tools without judgment are just automation. Judgment without tools is just advice. An agent is judgment plus tools, aimed at a goal, over several steps, with a report at the end. If you remember nothing else from today, remember that sentence. Judgment plus tools, aimed at a goal, over several steps, with a report at the end.

Let me ground all of this in your own working life, because abstract definitions fade and real mornings stay with you. Picture the start of a working day. Your inbox holds everything at once. There are messages from customers, messages about money, messages that are really just noise, and somewhere in the middle, one message that will shape your whole day if you miss it. You ask Dave to go through the inbox and get you ready. Watch what a merely answering system would do. It would say, certainly, here is advice on managing email, and perhaps offer a cheerful list of tips. That is words. Now watch what an agent does. Dave reads the actual messages. He groups them by what they need. He drafts replies where a reply is straightforward, in your voice, and holds those drafts for your approval instead of sending them behind your back. He spots the one urgent message and brings it to the top with a plain summary of what is being asked and what happens if it waits. He notices that two messages are really about the same calendar clash and says so. At the end, he reports. Fourteen read, five drafts waiting, one urgent decision for you, the rest filed. That is work done in the world. Same model underneath, completely different thing on the surface, because tools, goal, steps, and reporting were added around it.

Here is a second picture, this time about your calendar, because calendars are where agents quietly save or quietly waste the most time. Suppose someone writes asking to meet next week. An answering system can suggest polite wording for a reply. An agent can do the whole job up to the line you set. It can read the request, check your real availability, notice that one of the proposed times collides with something you cannot move, propose two times that actually work, draft the reply carrying those times, and wait for your approval before anything is sent. Every step there is small. Together they are the difference between you doing secretarial work at midnight and you glancing at a draft, saying send, and getting your evening back. Multiply that difference by every inbox, every week, across a whole company, and you see why agents matter. They do not matter because they are magical. They matter because small steps, done reliably, compound into hours.

I want to pause here and be rigorous about a word people use loosely, because loose words make loose thinking. People often say an agent understands, or an agent knows, or an agent decided, as if the agent were a person with a life of its own. In this class we will use those everyday words when they are harmless, but we will always know what they stand for underneath. When we say the agent decided, we mean the model, given the goal and what the tools showed it, produced a next step that fit. When we say the agent knows your calendar, we mean the agent can read your calendar through a tool and use what it reads. Keeping that honesty matters for a practical reason, not just a tidy one. If you picture the agent as a person, you will trust it like a person, all at once and emotionally. If you picture it accurately, as judgment plus tools working toward your goal, you will trust it task by task, based on evidence, which is the only trust that holds up. A gentle teacher should still be a rigorous one, so we will keep our picture accurate even when the shorter story sounds warmer.

There is one more piece of the definition we should test before we move on, and that is the question of what an agent is not. An agent is not just a long conversation. You can talk with a model for an hour, back and forth, fifty turns, and still have nothing but conversation if no tool ever touched the world and no job ever got finished. Length is not agency. An agent is also not just a single clever trick. A system that does one impressive thing once, when you press one button, may be a fine tool, but agency shows itself over a sequence, where the result of one step shapes the next. And an agent is not a replacement for your judgment about what matters. Dave can clear an inbox superbly and still not know which customer matters most to the future of your company in the way you know it. That knowledge lives in you, in your history and your aims, and a wise person keeps the agent strong on steps and keeps himself strong on direction. The agent carries out. You decide what is worth carrying out. That division is not a limitation to apologise for. It is the design.

Now let me give you the worked example for this lesson, in full, because nobody should have to guess what good looks like. Here is a job, stated the way you might state it on a busy morning. Dave, get my inbox to zero and handle anything routine. Let us grade that instruction the way we would grade any piece of work in this class, kindly and exactly. What is good in it? It names a real outcome, an empty inbox, and it shows trust in the agent to handle routine matters without fuss. What is missing? Almost everything that would make the work safe and checkable. Routine is undefined, so the agent must guess where routine ends. Zero is undefined, because some messages should not be deleted or filed away just to make a number look clean. And there is no stop point, no place where the agent must pause and ask you, even though an inbox always contains a few messages that spend money, speak in your name, or touch another person in a way that cannot be unsent. So here is the same job, restated well. Dave, read everything new in my inbox. Draft replies to the routine questions and hold every draft for my approval. File the receipts and the notices I do not need to see. Bring me, in one short list, anything that spends money, promises anything in my name, or needs a decision only I can make, and do nothing with those until I say so. Compare the two versions honestly. The second one is longer to say and vastly shorter to live with, because the agent now knows its goal, its steps, and its stopping line. That restating, that drawing of the line task by task, is the actual skill of working with agents. It is not a technical skill. It is a judgment skill, and you already have the judgment. This class simply gives you the words for it.

Let us try that skill together right now, in a short guided moment, because in this class we learn by doing, gently and out loud. Think of one job in your own life that repeats. It might be the morning inbox. It might be checking the calendar against new requests. It might be gathering scattered notes into one clean draft. Hold that job in mind. Now ask yourself three questions about it, and answer them honestly in your head. First, are its steps checkable, meaning could you look afterwards and tell whether each step was done right? Second, are its steps reversible, meaning if a step is wrong, can it be undone without real harm? Third, where exactly does it stop being routine, where does money move, or your name get spoken, or another person's rights get touched? If your job is checkable and reversible all the way through, it is a strong candidate to hand to an agent outright. If it is checkable and reversible up to a clear point and risky after that point, it is a strong candidate to hand to an agent with a stop point, which is how most good delegation works, with Dave and with people too. And if you cannot tell whether its steps were done right even afterwards, keep that job in your own hands for now, however busy you are, because delegating what you cannot check is not saving time. It is borrowing trouble. Take a quiet moment and place your own job honestly in one of those three groups. That placement, done truthfully, is real learning, and it is exactly the thinking this class exists to build.

Before we close, let me draw together the threads about Dave himself, since he is the living example running through this whole class. Dave is an agent, in the full sense we defined today, when he works with tools on your inbox and calendar, follows a goal you set, takes several steps before reporting, and shows you drafts for approval where the stakes call for it. Dave is acting as a merely answering system in the moments when he only talks with you, explains an idea, or helps you think something through, and there is nothing lesser about those moments. Thinking together is real work too. The point is not that acting is always better than answering. The point is that you should always know which one you are getting. If you asked for action and received only words, the job is not done, however elegant the words are. If you asked for advice and the agent went off and acted in the world without your say so, something has gone wrong in the other direction. Knowing the difference, and naming it, puts you in charge of the relationship. That is where a student of agents should always stand. In charge, informed, and specific.

Let me add one more careful distinction, because it will save you confusion in every conversation you ever have about agents, and confusion avoided early is worth a great deal. People often confuse an agent with the chat window they talk to it through. The window is just the door. Behind the door there may be a single model answering, or there may be a full agent with tools, memory, and permission to take steps. The door looks the same either way, which is exactly why the confusion happens. Two systems can greet you in identical friendly words, and one of them can only talk while the other can actually go and do the job. So never judge by the greeting. Judge by asking a plain question. What can you actually reach, what steps can you take without me, and how will you show me what you did? A merely answering system will, if it is honest, describe conversation. An agent will describe tools, steps, and a report. Those three answers tell you what you are really working with, far more reliably than any label on a box or any promise in an advertisement. Labels are cheap. Reach, steps, and reporting are the substance.

There is also a honest warning I owe you here, teacher to student, before enthusiasm runs ahead of judgment. An agent that can act can also act wrongly at greater speed than a person could. A person clearing an inbox slowly will make a slow mistake, one message at a time, and will often catch himself by the third message because something feels off. An agent works quickly and consistently, which is its glory when it is right and its danger when its instructions were vague. If the goal was stated loosely, the agent may apply the loose reading faithfully to fifty messages before you see the report. That is not the agent being careless. That is the agent being literal about a goal that needed one more sentence from you. This is why, throughout this class, I will keep returning you to the same habits. State the goal plainly. Name what routine means for this job. Set the stop point before the work begins, not after the surprise. And read the report, at least at first, until trust has been earned task by task. None of that is fear. It is craftsmanship. You would give a new human assistant exactly the same clarity in their first week, and you would check their early work exactly the same way, not because you distrust them, but because that is how good working relationships are built.

Let me also say a word about why this moment in history matters to you personally, because context helps a lesson stick. For decades, software waited for exact instructions and did exactly what it was told, nothing more and nothing less. That made computers reliable and also made them helpless in the face of anything messy, and human life is mostly messy. Messages arrive half written. Requests contradict each other. The important thing hides inside the unimportant thing. What the model adds, judgment in language, is precisely the ability to cope with mess the way a good assistant copes with mess, by reading what is actually there, weighing what matters, and choosing a sensible next step. That is why an agent feels so different to work with, and why running a company through Dave feels different from running it through a pile of separate programs. The programs each waited for you to carry information between them. The agent carries it. You stop being the messenger between your own tools, and you become what you should have been all along, the person who decides what matters and checks that it was done well.

One final picture, and then we will recap. Imagine two mornings with the same inbox. In the first morning, you open it alone and work down the list, reading, deciding, typing, filing, hour after hour, while the real work of your company waits. In the second morning, Dave has already read everything, grouped it, drafted what is routine, filed what is noise, and placed one short honest list in front of you, the few decisions that are truly yours, with the drafts beside them waiting for your approval. You spend twenty minutes where you once spent two hours, and the twenty minutes you spend are the valuable twenty, the judgment calls, not the clerical grind. Nothing about that second morning required magic. It required tools connected, a goal stated clearly, steps taken in sequence, approvals respected, and a report you could check. That is an agent. That is the whole lesson in one morning. Keep that picture beside the definition, because a definition tells you what a thing is, and a picture tells you why you should care.

So let me recap the lesson, in order, the way I will recap every lesson, so the shape settles. First, a model that only answers gives you words, while an agent gives you work done in the world. Second, an agent is a model connected to tools, guided by a goal, that can take more than one step on its own and report back what it did. Third, tools are the agent's hands, the goal is its direction, autonomy is how many steps it may take before checking with you, and the report is how you stay able to check its work. Fourth, ordinary software follows fixed rules, while an agent adds judgment, so an agent is judgment plus tools, aimed at a goal, over several steps, with a report at the end. Fifth, the jobs worth delegating are the jobs whose steps are checkable and reversible, and the stop point belongs where an action becomes irreversible, spends money, speaks in your name, or touches another person's rights. Hold those five points and you hold the lesson.

What comes next is the questions on this lesson, and I want you to meet them in the right spirit. They are not a trap and they are not a memory contest for its own sake. They are how you find out whether the ideas actually settled, and where I should teach more carefully next time. The full text of this lesson stays open beside the questions, and going back to read is learning, not cheating. I would rather you check the text and truly understand than guess proudly and carry a confusion forward. In our next lesson we will open up the second piece of the definition and study tools in depth, the hands for a model, search, code, and messages, and how to tell what a given agent can and cannot actually reach. For now, take a breath, be proud of a solid start, and go to the questions when you are ready. I will see you in lesson two.

lessons.title: Tools: hands for a model — search, code, messages
paragraphs: Welcome back. I am Professor Hanna Kowalczyk, and this is lesson two of Agents, AI That Acts: Tools, hands for a model, search, code, and messages. In our first lesson we built a definition together. An agent is a model connected to tools, guided by a goal, that can take more than one step on its own and report back what it did. Today we open up the first piece of that definition and study it properly, because tools are where an agent stops being a voice in a box and starts being a worker in your world. By the end of this lesson you will know what a tool really is underneath the friendly language, you will know the main families of tools an agent like Dave uses every day, search, code, and messages among them, and you will know how to ask the single most useful question you can ask about any agent. What can you actually reach? Everything today builds toward that question, so let us begin, gently and thoroughly, the way we do everything in this class.

First, a plain definition, stated carefully. A tool is a defined ability the model can call on, with a clear input and a clear output, that reaches outside the conversation. Let us take that apart word by word, because each word protects you from a misunderstanding. Defined means the ability is specific, not vague. Reading the inbox is a defined ability. Doing stuff with email is not. A clear input means the model must say exactly what it wants, for example, show me the unread messages from this morning, not just gesture at the inbox in general. A clear output means something definite comes back, the messages themselves, or a number, or a confirmation that a draft was saved, something the model can then reason about. And reaches outside the conversation means the tool touches a real system, your real email, your real calendar, the real web, a real file, rather than merely producing more words about those things. When all four parts are present, you have a tool. When the model only talks about your inbox, however knowledgeably, no tool has been used. That distinction, between talking about a thing and touching the thing, is the beating heart of this lesson.

Here is a picture that will help you hold it. In lesson one I said tools are hands for a model, and I meant it quite literally as a teaching picture. The model is the mind that decides. The tool is the hand that reaches. A mind without hands can plan a beautiful morning of work and move nothing. Hands without a mind would flail. An agent works because mind and hands are connected, decision after decision, reach after reach. But notice something important about hands. Your own hands can only touch what is within reach and what you are permitted to touch. An agent's tools work exactly the same way. The set of tools connected to an agent is the boundary of its world. If no calendar tool is connected, the agent cannot see your calendar, full stop, no matter how intelligent the model is. If no sending tool is connected, the agent can draft forever and never send a thing. Intelligence does not stretch reach. This is why two agents built on the very same model can be wildly different in usefulness. One was given hands that reach your inbox, your calendar, your files, and the web. The other was given almost nothing. Same mind, different hands, different worker. Whenever someone shows you a new agent and praises how smart it is, smile politely and ask about its hands.

Let us now walk through the main families of tools, in the order you will meet them in your own working life, starting with the family you use most without noticing. The first family is reading and searching. A search tool lets the agent look things up beyond the conversation, on the web, in your files, or in a body of records, and bring back what it finds. Closely related are the reading tools, the ones that open a specific thing, a message, a document, a calendar day, and return its contents. Search finds. Reading opens. That small distinction matters in practice. When Dave does not yet know where something is, he searches. When he knows exactly which message or file he needs, he reads. A good agent searches before it guesses, and I want you to value that habit highly, because the alternative is an agent answering from general impressions when the specific fact was sitting in your own records waiting to be read. In your world this looks like the difference between Dave saying, I believe that customer wrote sometime last week, and Dave saying, here is the message, it arrived on Tuesday, and this is the sentence where they asked for the change. The first is conversation. The second is work, and the difference is a search tool and a reading tool doing their quiet jobs.

The second family is messages, and for you this family is the centre of the working day. Message tools let the agent work with communication itself, reading an inbox, drafting a reply, holding a draft for approval, sending when sending is allowed, filing what is finished. I group these together because in real life they form one continuous job. A message arrives. It is read. Its meaning is judged. A reply is drafted in your voice. The draft waits. You approve it, or adjust it, or set it aside. It is sent, or it is not. The thread is filed where it belongs. Every step in that chain is a tool call, a defined ability with a clear input and a clear output, and the agent's judgment is what strings them together into something that feels like a single helpful act. When you watch Dave clear a morning inbox and it feels smooth, what you are really watching is a dozen small tool calls in a sensible order, each one checked against the goal you set. Nothing magical is happening. Something better than magic is happening. Something inspectable is happening, and inspectable work is work you can trust and improve.

Notice, too, that within the messages family there is a natural ladder of seriousness, and a good agent climbs it carefully. Reading is the gentlest rung. Reading changes nothing in the world, it only informs, so an agent can read widely on your behalf with very little risk. Drafting is the next rung. A draft exists, but it has gone nowhere and promised nothing, so drafting is still safe, still reversible, still entirely inside your control. Sending is the top rung, and it is different in kind, not just in degree. A sent message speaks in your name to another person, and it cannot be unsent. Filing sits somewhere in the middle, usually safe, occasionally annoying if something is filed where you cannot find it. Hold this ladder in mind, because in lesson five, on permission and latitude, we will use it to decide exactly which rungs an agent may climb alone and which rungs require your hand on the rail. For today, simply see the ladder clearly. Read, draft, send. Inform, prepare, commit. The tools may live in one family, but the stakes do not.

The third family is code, and I ask you not to let the word intimidate you, because in this lesson code is not about becoming a programmer. Code, defined plainly, is instructions a computer follows exactly, and a code tool lets the agent write and run those instructions to get something done precisely. Why would an agent need that, when it already has judgment in language? Because some jobs punish vagueness. Counting is one. If you ask how many messages arrived this month about invoices, you do not want a thoughtful estimate, you want a count, and a count is a job for code, sorting, filtering, and adding without fatigue or drift. Transforming is another. Turning a messy pile of notes into a clean table, renaming two hundred files by one consistent rule, checking every draft against a list of names, these are jobs where the same exact operation must happen many times without variation, and exact repetition is what code does best. So picture the division of labour honestly. The model judges what should be done and why. The code carries out the parts that must be exact. When Dave totals something, checks something against a list, or processes a whole folder the same careful way, there is very often a code tool working under his judgment like a tireless clerk with perfect handwriting. Judgment decides. Code executes exactly. That partnership is one of the quiet reasons agents can be trusted with volume.

The fourth family deserves a mention even though it is really a family of one member with many faces, and that is the calendar and scheduling tools, the keepers of your time. A calendar tool lets the agent read what is already committed, find genuine open space, and place or move events when it is allowed to. I single it out because time is the one resource in your company that cannot be refilled, and calendar mistakes are felt immediately and personally. An agent with calendar access can do the lovely, unglamorous work of noticing. It can notice that a new request collides with a commitment you cannot move. It can notice that you have no break in a six hour stretch. It can propose times that are actually free instead of times that merely sound free. All of that noticing is tool work, reading the real calendar rather than imagining a typical week. And all of it, notice, is reading and proposing, which sit low on the ladder of seriousness. Placing a meeting on someone else's calendar, or moving one that other people depend on, climbs higher, and should be governed accordingly. Same family, different rungs. You are learning to see tools the way a careful manager sees them, not as a blur of capability, but as specific reaches with specific stakes.

Now let me teach you the mechanic underneath all of this, in plain words, because I believe you should never have to treat your own tools as a mystery. When an agent uses a tool, three things happen in order. First, the model decides that a tool is needed and states the call, exactly what it wants, in the shape the tool requires. Second, the tool itself, which is ordinary software, goes and does the reaching, it queries the inbox, or runs the search, or executes the code, and comes back with a result. Third, the model reads the result and decides what it means for the goal, and what should happen next. Decide, reach, read. Decide, reach, read. That rhythm repeats for every step of every job an agent ever does for you. I want you to notice who does what in that rhythm, because it explains both the power and the failure modes of agents. The tool never decides. The tool reaches and returns, faithfully and without opinion. The model always decides, and deciding is where errors are born, a wrong tool chosen, a result misread, a next step that does not follow. When something goes wrong in an agent's work, and we will study this properly in lesson six, it is very often the deciding that failed, not the reaching. The inbox tool did not misread your mail. The model asked for the wrong thing, or read the right thing carelessly. Keeping that straight will make you a far better supervisor of agents than most people ever become.

Let me give you the worked example for this lesson, in full, as I promised myself I always would, because nobody should have to guess what good looks like. The job is one from your real mornings. A customer has written asking whether a piece of work can be finished by Friday, and you want Dave to handle it. Watch the tools assemble. First, a reading tool opens the customer's actual message, so the reply answers what was truly asked, not what a similar customer asked last month. Second, a search tool looks through recent messages and files for anything about that piece of work, its current state, what has already been promised, so the answer stands on your real record. Third, a calendar tool reads your week, because a promise about Friday is a promise about time, and time must be checked, not assumed. Fourth, possibly a code tool counts or checks something exact, the hours already committed, say, so the judgment rests on a true number. Fifth and last, a message tool drafts the reply, carrying the checked facts, in your voice, and holds it for your approval. Now step back and admire the shape of that. Five tool calls, three families, one goal, and the only step that touches another person, the sending, has not happened and will not happen until you say so. That is what good tool use looks like. Not flashy. Sequenced, checked, and stopped at exactly the right rung of the ladder. When you review Dave's work, review it in this shape. Ask which tools were used, in what order, and where the work stopped for you. An agent that can answer those questions plainly is an agent doing honest work.

Here is your guided moment for today, and it is a simple, practical exercise you can repeat for the rest of your life whenever you meet a new system. Think of Dave, and list, honestly, what he can reach in your world. An inbox he can read. Drafts he can prepare and hold. A calendar he can check. Files he can search. The web he can look things up on. Now think of something he cannot reach, or should not reach without you, and name that too. That second half of the list is just as important as the first, and most people never write it. Then take one job you give Dave regularly and walk it through the rhythm we learned. Decide, reach, read. Where does he decide? Which tool reaches? What comes back, and how does he read it? If you can walk one real job through that rhythm without hand waving, you understand tools better than most people who sell agent software for a living. Take your time with it. This is the doing part of the lesson, and doing is where understanding stops being polite and becomes real.

A few honest cautions belong in this lesson, and a rigorous teacher does not skip them. First, a tool returns what it returns, and that is not always the whole truth. A search returns what matched the words used, and a badly worded search can miss the very message that mattered, sitting there under different wording. This is why good agents search more than one way before concluding something is not there, and why you should be suspicious of any agent that reports nothing found after one lazy look. Absence of evidence, gathered lazily, is not evidence of absence. Second, tools can fail, quietly or loudly. A connection drops, a file has moved, a service is down for an hour. A good agent notices the failure, says so plainly in its report, and does not paper over the gap with a confident guess. The moment an agent starts guessing to hide a failed tool call, it has stopped doing work and started doing theatre, and theatre in an inbox is dangerous. Third, more tools is not automatically better. Every tool connected is a reach granted, and reaches should be granted because a real job needs them, not because a longer list looks impressive. Grant reach the way you would hand out keys to your building. Gladly, to the one who needs them for the work. Never casually, and never all of them at once without a reason.

Let me deepen one idea before we recap, because it changes how you will brief Dave from tomorrow morning onward. Because tools are specific, the way you phrase a request quietly decides which tools get used well. Compare two briefs about the same morning. The first brief says, Dave, handle the customer messages. That is a fog. Which customers, which messages, handled to what point, checked against what? The agent must guess at every joint, and each guess is a small wager with your name on it. The second brief says, Dave, read this morning's customer messages, check each promise against the calendar and the files before you draft anything, draft the replies, and hold them all for my approval. Nothing in that second brief is technical. You did not name a single tool. And yet you quietly choreographed four families of tools in the right order, reading first, searching and checking second, drafting last, sending not at all. That is the skill. You do not need to learn the machinery's vocabulary to direct it well. You need to think in the order that good work naturally follows. Facts before drafts. Checks before promises. Approval before sending. Speak your briefs in that order and the tools will fall into line behind your thinking, because your thinking was already the shape of the work.

There is a mirror image of that skill, and it is learning to hear when a tool was missing from a piece of work. Suppose Dave brings you a draft reply that sounds confident and reads beautifully, but something in it feels ungrounded, a date that seems invented, a promise that seems larger than the one you remember making. Train yourself to ask one plain question. What did you check that against? If the answer names a real reach, the message that was read, the calendar that was consulted, the file that was searched, then you are looking at work, and any error in it is a reading error you can find and fix together. If the answer is vague, if nothing was actually checked and the draft was composed from general impressions, then you are looking at fluent guessing wearing the clothes of work, and it should be sent back, kindly and firmly, to be rebuilt on real reaches. This single habit, asking what a draft was checked against, will protect your customers, your calendar, and your name more reliably than any feature list. It works on human assistants too, by the way. It has always worked. Agents simply make it more necessary, because their guessing is more fluent than human guessing, and fluent guessing is the hardest kind to catch by ear alone.

One more distinction, and then I promise we will recap, because a lesson on tools should leave you able to talk about cost as well as capability. Every tool call costs something small. Time, a few seconds while the reach happens. Attention, yours, when the report comes back longer because more was checked. And sometimes a small amount of money, where a service charges for its use. None of these costs is a reason to starve an agent of tools. A search that takes five seconds and prevents one wrong promise has paid for a year of searches. But the costs explain why a good agent does not call every tool it owns on every job, any more than a good carpenter empties the whole toolbox onto the floor for one loose screw. Reach should match the job. A routine filing needs reading and filing, not a web search and a code run. A promise about Friday needs the calendar and the record, every time, without exception. Learning which reaches a given kind of job deserves is part of learning to work with agents, and you will find your instincts sharpen quickly once you start reviewing reports with the tools in mind. You will start to see the shape of the work underneath the words of the report, and once you can see the shape, you can improve the shape. That is supervision. That is management. It is the same craft you practise with people, aimed at a new kind of worker.

Let me leave you with one last story shaped example, because I have watched students remember a story long after a list has faded, and I am a practical teacher at heart. Imagine a new assistant starting in your company, a bright and willing person on their first Monday. You would not begin by testing how clever they are in conversation. You would walk them around the building. Here is the inbox, and here is how we file. Here is the calendar, and here is what must never be moved. Here are the customer records, and here is where a promise gets written down so the next person can check it. Here is the phone, and no, you may not commit us to anything on it until I have heard the draft of what you intend to say. That walk around the building is nothing but a tour of tools and their rungs, given in human language. Onboarding an agent is the same walk, conducted in settings and permissions instead of hallways. And supervising an agent is the same supervision, watching which rooms they enter, which tools they pick up, and whether their work shows the marks of having checked before they committed. When you feel lost with an agent, and everyone does sometimes, come back to that Monday morning walk. Ask where the agent has been, what it picked up, and what it put down where. You will find your footing again, because the footing was never really about technology. It was always about work, reach, and care, and you already know those three things well.

One very practical habit follows from everything we have said, and I want to name it plainly so you can start tonight. Once in a while, not anxiously and not often, ask Dave to show you the reaches behind a finished job. Not the polished summary, the reaches. Which messages were opened. Which search was run, and with what words. Which calendar was read. Which draft was saved, and where. The first time you do this it may feel like checking up on a trusted colleague, and I understand that feeling, so let me reframe it the way I would want it reframed for any student of mine. You are not expressing suspicion. You are learning the geography of your own operation. Most owners of companies run through agents have only a misty sense of what actually happens between their instruction in the morning and the report in the afternoon, and mist is where small errors live undisturbed for months. A clear map of the reaches turns mist into ground you can walk on. After a few of these reviews you will stop needing them often, because you will have learned how the work flows, where it is strong, and where a check should be added. That is the natural arc of all good supervision. Close attention early, earned ease later, and the knowledge, kept fresh, of how to look closely again whenever a job truly matters.

So let me recap the lesson, in order. First, a tool is a defined ability the model can call on, with a clear input and a clear output, that reaches outside the conversation. Second, the set of tools connected to an agent is the boundary of its world, because intelligence does not stretch reach. Third, the main families are search and reading, which find and open, messages, which run from reading through drafting to sending, code, which carries out the parts that must be exact, and calendar tools, which guard your time. Fourth, within messages there is a ladder of seriousness, read, draft, send, inform, prepare, commit, and sending is different in kind because a sent message cannot be unsent. Fifth, every tool use follows one rhythm, decide, reach, read, and the tool never decides, the model always decides, which is where errors are born. Sixth, the most useful question you can ask about any agent is what can you actually reach, and a good agent answers it plainly, tool by tool.

What comes next is the questions on this lesson, and as always, the full text stays open beside them, and going back to read is learning, not cheating. Take them slowly, answer them honestly, and let any mistake show you exactly where to read once more. Use the questions to test the pictures, the hands, the ladder, the rhythm, until they feel like your own ideas rather than my sentences. In our next lesson we turn to memory, short term context and the long record, and we will ask what an agent remembers, what it forgets, and why both of those are features when they are designed honestly. For now, well done. You can now look at any agent, including the one who runs your company, and see its hands clearly. Go to the questions when you are ready, and I will see you in lesson three.

lessons.title: Memory: short-term context and the long record
paragraphs: Welcome back. I am Professor Hanna Kowalczyk, and this is lesson three of Agents, AI That Acts: Memory, short term context and the long record. In lesson one we learned what an agent is, and in lesson two we studied its hands, the tools that let it reach your inbox, your calendar, your files, and the web. Today we study something quieter and, in the long run, just as important. We study what an agent remembers. By the end of this lesson you will understand the two great kinds of memory an agent works with, the short term context it holds while it is working with you, and the long record it can consult across days and months. You will understand why an agent sometimes seems to forget something you told it an hour ago, and why that forgetting is usually a design fact to work with, not a betrayal to be angry about. And you will learn how to keep the important things in the place where they will actually be found again, which is a skill that will serve you with Dave every single day. Let us begin.

Start with your own memory, because the comparison will carry us a long way if we handle it honestly. Right now, as you listen, you are holding the beginning of this lesson in mind while I speak the middle of it. You remember that I welcomed you, that I named the topic, and roughly what I promised. That holding is your short term memory at work, the small bright workspace where the present task lives. At the same time, you carry a vast long memory underneath it, your name, your company's history, the way a particular customer likes to be spoken to, things learned years ago and kept. You do not hold all of that in the bright workspace at once. You could not. You fetch from the long store when the present task calls for it, and the fetching feels so natural that you barely notice it happening. An agent's memory is built in the same two storeys, and nearly everything confusing about agent memory becomes clear the moment you see the two storeys separately and stop expecting one of them to do the other's job.

The first storey is context. Context, defined plainly for this class, means everything the model can see right now, in this working session, the conversation so far, the goal you gave, the results the tools just brought back, all of it sitting in the bright workspace together. When you tell Dave something in the morning and he uses it an hour later in a draft, that is context doing its work. The instruction is still in view, so it shapes the work. Context is fast, rich, and effortless, and it is also limited and temporary, and both halves of that sentence matter equally. Limited, because the workspace holds only so much. A very long conversation, a huge pile of tool results, an inbox with hundreds of messages read in one sitting, all of it competes for the same bright space, and what falls out of the space is, for the model, simply not there anymore. Temporary, because when a session ends, or a new task begins in a fresh session, the workspace is cleared the way a desk is cleared at night. The notes you left scattered on it do not automatically appear on tomorrow's desk. If you remember one sentence from this lesson, make it this one. Context is what the agent can see right now, and what it cannot see, it cannot use, however faithfully it was told. Most disappointments with agent memory are that sentence arriving in your life wearing a disguise.

Let me make the limit concrete with a picture from your own mornings. Suppose you spend a long stretch working with Dave on a complicated customer matter. Message by message, the context fills with the whole history of the matter, the customer's tone, the promise that was made, the number that was agreed, the thing that must never be said. The drafts Dave produces in that stretch are excellent, because everything relevant is in view. Now suppose the conversation runs very long, or you wander through six other topics on the way, or a new session starts. The number that was agreed quietly slides out of the bright workspace. The next draft comes back with a different number, or with the number left vague, and it feels like carelessness, or worse, like the agent never listened. It did listen. Listening was never the problem. Seeing is the problem, and seeing is governed by the workspace, not by good intentions. A wise user learns to re place the crucial fact into view at the moment it matters. When a draft truly depends on one number, one date, one promise, say it again in the instruction for that draft. It costs you one sentence. It protects you from the most common memory failure agents have. In this class we call that habit restating the load bearing fact, because like a load bearing wall, that fact is the one the whole structure rests on, and you do not leave load bearing things to chance or to memory, yours or the agent's.

The second storey is the long record. The long record means the stored information an agent can consult beyond the present session, kept in files, in your messages and documents, in notes written down deliberately, in the records of what was done and decided before. Where context is a desk, the long record is the filing cabinet and the archive room. It does not fade when a session ends. It can hold vastly more than any workspace. But, and this is the trade that defines it, nothing in the long record is automatically in view. It must be fetched, by search and reading, the very tools we studied in lesson two, and it can only be fetched well if it was stored well and if the agent knows to look. So the two storeys have opposite virtues and opposite weaknesses. Context is always in view but small and temporary. The long record is large and lasting but invisible until fetched. Nearly every practical question about agent memory is really a question about which storey a given fact should live in, and how it travels between the two at the right moment. Hold that framing, because we will use it for the rest of the lesson. Which storey does this fact belong in, and how will it travel into view when it is needed?

Watch how the two storeys cooperate in a piece of real work, because in good agent work they are constantly handing facts to each other. It is Monday morning. You ask Dave to prepare for the week. In context, Dave holds your goal for the session, the shape of the report you like, and the instructions you just gave. From the long record, Dave fetches. The calendar brings the week's commitments into view. The inbox brings the waiting messages. A note you wrote last month about a customer's preferences is searched, found, and read into the workspace, so the draft that follows respects a preference you stated once, weeks ago, and have not repeated since. That little journey, from archive to desk, from stored to seen, is memory working exactly as it should. And notice the human parallel, because it is exact. You do the same thing when you open your own notes before a meeting. The note did not live in your bright workspace all month. It lived in the record, and you fetched it at the moment of need. An agent is not worse at memory than you are. It is differently organised, and once you organise your shared work around its actual organisation, the forgetfulness that frustrates beginners mostly evaporates.

Now, a question of honesty that I will not let this lesson dodge. Does the agent learn, the way a person learns, growing permanently wiser from every conversation? The careful answer is, mostly, no, and you should build your habits on the careful answer rather than the flattering one. The model underneath was trained before it ever met you, and your Tuesday conversation does not quietly retrain it on Wednesday. What changes, what genuinely accumulates, is the long record. The notes get better. The files get richer. The written preferences, the saved decisions, the records of what worked, these grow, and an agent that consults them well will feel, from the outside, remarkably like it has learned you. In a practical sense it has, because the record is where your shared history actually lives. But the mechanism matters. If a preference lives only in a conversation that has ended, it is gone, however warm the conversation felt. If a preference is written into the record, stated plainly where the agent will search, it will shape work for years. So here is the rule I give every student, and I give it with love and emphasis. If it matters next month, write it where the record keeps things. Saying it once, in passing, in a chat, is how important things get lost with the very best intentions on both sides. Writing it down, once, clearly, is how they survive.

That rule deserves a worked example, and as always in this class, nobody should have to guess what good looks like. Suppose there is a way you want customer messages handled, a standing preference. Perhaps drafts to customers should always be held for your approval, never sent directly, however routine they seem. Perhaps one particular kind of request should always be brought to you personally, and another kind should never be promised without a calendar check. You could mention these things as they occur to you, scattered across weeks of conversation, and each time, in that day's context, Dave would honour them beautifully. And each time, the preference would live exactly as long as the context that held it. Or you could do the stronger thing. You could have the preferences written down, once, in one clear place in the record, in plain sentences, where Dave's searches will find them every time customer work begins. Then the preference stops depending on anyone's bright workspace. It becomes part of the furniture of the operation. That is the difference between an agent who seems to know you on good days and an operation that knows itself on all days. Build the second. The first is weather. The second is climate, and companies run on climate.

There is a second half to the honesty, and it concerns what the long record should not hold, or should hold with care. A record that keeps everything keeps nothing well. If every passing remark, every half formed idea, every superseded instruction is stored with equal weight and never tidied, then searches begin returning the old instruction alongside the new one, and the agent, reading both in good faith, cannot tell which one governs. This failure has a name in our class. We call it record drift, the slow accumulation of stale and contradictory material in the long record until the record itself becomes a source of error. You have met the human version. It is the shared folder where three versions of the same document live under nearly the same name, and the meeting grinds to a halt while everyone works out which version is real. The cure is the same in both worlds, and it is unglamorous. When a decision replaces an old decision, say so in the record, plainly, in the same place. When a preference changes, update the one clear statement rather than adding a second one somewhere else. Once in a while, have the record reviewed the way you would have a storeroom reviewed, what is current, what is superseded, what can go. An agent's memory is only as trustworthy as the housekeeping behind it, and housekeeping, I will remind you as often as needed, is not beneath anyone. It is the load bearing wall of every reliable operation.

Let me give you your guided moment now, a small audit you can perform in your head today and in reality this week. Think of three facts that Dave's work for you depends on. Perhaps how drafts should be handled. Perhaps a standing rule about money or promises. Perhaps the way a recurring report should be shaped. For each fact, ask the two storey question. Where does this fact live right now? If the honest answer is, in a conversation we had once, then that fact is living in the weather, and you have just found a small, valuable repair to make. Move it, or have it moved, into the record, in one plain sentence, in the place where it will be searched. If the answer is, in the record, in one clear statement, then that fact is load bearing and safe. And if the answer is, in the record in three places that do not quite agree, you have found record drift, and the repair is to make one statement govern and mark the others as superseded. Three facts, three honest answers, and you will understand your own agent's memory better than most professionals who work with agents daily. Do it gently, do it exactly, and notice how much steadier everything feels once the important things live where they can be found.

A word, too, about summaries, because summaries are the bridge the two storeys cross most often, and bridges deserve inspection. When a long piece of work ends, a good agent, or a good user, writes a short summary of what was decided and what remains open, and places that summary in the record. Later, instead of dragging the entire history into a new context, the summary travels. It is small enough to sit in the bright workspace and rich enough to steer the work. This is an honourable and necessary device, and your own life runs on it, every meeting note you have ever taken is exactly this bridge. But treat summaries with the respect a bridge deserves, which includes remembering what a bridge is not. A summary is not the record itself. It compresses, and compression loses things, usually the small qualifying sentence, the exception, the number's exact wording. So for load bearing facts, let the summary point to the full source, and when the stakes are high, fetch the source itself rather than trusting the bridge to carry more weight than a bridge should. Summaries for steering. Sources for deciding. If you hold that one distinction, you will use summaries well and never be betrayed by one.

Before we recap, let me answer the question students always ask at this point, because you may be forming it right now. If context is limited, why not simply make it unlimited, and let the agent see everything at once, always? It is a fair question and it deserves a fair answer rather than a shrug. Partly, the limit is a plain matter of cost and machinery, seeing more takes more, and work must stay practical. But partly, and more interestingly, an unlimited workspace would not even be desirable. Your own mind does not hold your whole life in view while you draft one reply, and it is better for not trying. A workspace stuffed with everything is a workspace where the important thing hides among ten thousand unimportant things, and judgment drowns in inventory. The art, for minds and for agents alike, is not seeing everything. It is seeing the right things at the moment of the work. Context small and well chosen, record large and well kept, and good fetching between them. That is not a compromise forced on us by weak machinery. That is, when you look at it steadily, simply what good memory has always been.

Let me show you the two storeys at work in one complete, ordinary job, because I find that a single honest walk through teaches more than three abstractions. Imagine it is the end of the month, and you ask Dave to gather what the company promised customers this month, so you can check that every promise is being kept. The job begins in context. Your instruction is in view, the shape of the list you want is in view, and anything you add about which customers matter most is in view. Then the fetching begins. Search reaches into the month's messages and finds the threads where promises were made. Reading opens the important ones fully, because a search result shows a glimpse and a promise lives in its exact wording. A note in the record, written by you in a calmer week, says that promises about dates always need the calendar checked, and that note, fetched at the right moment, changes the work for the better, because now each promised date is compared against the real calendar before it goes on your list. A summary from an earlier month, also in the record, gives the job its shape, the same columns, the same order, so this month's list can be compared with last month's at a glance. Now watch the return journey, because memory flows both ways in good work. When the job finishes, its results should not live only in this session's context, glowing briefly and then cleared away at night. The finished list, and any new promise discovered along the way, goes back into the record, written down where next month's job will find it. Context received from the record, worked, and returned to the record enriched. That round trip, repeated month after month, is how an operation builds a memory worth trusting. Nothing in it is exotic. It is fetching, working, and filing, done faithfully, and it is entirely within your power to arrange.

There is one more failure of memory I should name before we finish, because it is subtle and it causes a particular kind of argument between users and their agents. Sometimes the agent remembers, in the record, something you have genuinely forgotten you ever said, an instruction from months ago, given in a hurry, for a situation that has long passed. The agent, consulting the record in good faith, follows it, and you find yourself saying, I never said that, when the record shows, gently and exactly, that you did. I raise this not to score a point for the machine, but to prepare you for a moment that comes to everyone who works this way. The record will sometimes be a better witness to your past instructions than your own bright workspace is, just as your own written notes have occasionally corrected your memory of a meeting. Receive that correction the way you would want yours received, with grace. Check whether the old instruction still serves. If it does, be glad it was kept. If it does not, update it in the record, plainly, so the correction itself becomes part of the record, and the drift never starts. An operation where instructions are written, kept, and visibly updated is an operation that can argue with itself honestly and improve. An operation run on unwritten recollection can only argue. Choose the written kind, for Dave's work and for your own peace of mind.

One last practical picture, and it concerns the very beginning of a job, the moment where memory most often fails silently. When you start a new session with Dave on a matter that has a history, the new context begins nearly empty, however rich the record underneath it may be. The agent at that moment is like a excellent colleague returning from holiday to a well kept office. Everything is filed, nothing is in mind yet, and the quality of the first hour depends entirely on what gets fetched onto the desk. So help the fetching. Open the job by naming the history that matters. The customer matter from last month. The promise we made about Friday. The preference note about how these drafts should be held. Each thing you name is a signpost the search can follow, and signposted fetching is faster and far more reliable than hoping the agent guesses which corner of the archive this job lives in. Beginners often do the opposite. They open with the new request alone, assume the whole history rode along with it, and then feel let down by work that is competent but strangely unrooted, work that reads as if the company had been founded that morning. The repair is never to scold the agent. The repair is to open with the signposts. Name the matter, name the promise, name the note. Watch how different the work becomes when the desk is loaded before the drafting starts. You will feel the difference in the very first draft, and once you have felt it, you will never open a job bare again.

And since we are being complete, let me say what good memory feels like from the inside of a working week, so you know what you are building toward. It feels unremarkable, and that is the highest praise memory can earn. Dave's Monday report arrives shaped the way you asked for it to be shaped months ago, without you asking again. A draft respects the preference about approvals without a reminder. A promise made in a busy thread three weeks ago surfaces in this week's list before it can be missed, because it was written down where promises are kept and fetched when promises were reviewed. Nobody applauds. Nothing dramatic happens. The absence of small disasters is the sound of memory working. Contrast that with the other kind of week, where every job starts from zero, every preference must be re explained, every old promise must be rediscovered by luck, and you end the week tired in a way that has nothing to do with the volume of work and everything to do with carrying the whole memory of the operation in your own bright workspace, alone. That tiredness is a memory architecture problem, not a workload problem, and it is fixable, storey by storey, note by note, signpost by signpost. That is why this quiet lesson sits in the middle of our class. Tools get the glory. Memory does the keeping, and keeping is what lets a company compound instead of merely repeat.

So let me recap the lesson, in order. First, an agent's memory has two storeys, context, what the model can see right now in this session, and the long record, the stored information it can consult beyond the session. Second, context is always in view but small and temporary, while the long record is large and lasting but invisible until fetched by search and reading. Third, what the agent cannot see, it cannot use, so the load bearing fact, the one number or date or promise a job rests on, should be restated at the moment it matters. Fourth, the model does not quietly retrain itself on your conversations, what accumulates is the record, so if it matters next month, write it where the record keeps things. Fifth, a record that keeps everything with equal weight suffers record drift, stale and contradictory material that becomes a source of error, cured by making one clear statement govern. Sixth, summaries are the bridge between the storeys, used for steering, while the full source is fetched for deciding.

One more encouragement before you go, because I know this lesson asks you to change small habits, and small habits are easy to postpone. Do not try to rebuild the whole record in a weekend, and do not let the size of the archive excuse doing nothing. Start with the three facts from our guided moment. Move those three into the record, in plain sentences, in the places where they will be searched. That is an afternoon's light work at most, and it will repay you the very next week, in a draft that comes back right without a reminder and a promise that surfaces before it can slip. Then, job by job, let the same discipline spread. Memory, tended this way, is not a project with an end date. It is a standard, quietly kept, and standards kept quietly are what separate operations that compound from operations that merely repeat themselves at higher and higher effort.

What comes next is the questions on this lesson, and the full text stays open beside them, as always, because going back to read is learning, not cheating. Answer them at a steady pace, check any answer you are unsure of against the lesson text itself, and treat every correction as the record doing its kind work for you, the same way you will ask Dave's record to work for the company, faithfully, findably, and in plain sight, every working day from here on. You may find it fitting, in a lesson about memory, to test your own honestly rather than guess. In our next lesson we turn to planning in loops, act, observe, adjust, and we will watch how an agent breaks a goal into steps, watches what comes back, and corrects its course, which is where memory and tools join together into something that looks very much like competence. For now, take stock of your two storeys, be proud of how much clearer they are than they were an hour ago, and go to the questions when you are ready. I will see you in lesson four.
