lessons.title: Planning in loops: act, observe, adjust
paragraphs: Welcome back. I am Professor Hanna Kowalczyk, and this is lesson four of Agents, AI That Acts: Planning in loops, act, observe, adjust. We have built our agent piece by piece. Lesson one gave us the definition, a model connected to tools, guided by a goal, taking more than one step on its own and reporting back. Lesson two studied the tools, the hands. Lesson three studied memory, the context in view and the long record underneath. Today we study the motion itself, the way an agent actually gets a real job done when the job is too big, too messy, or too uncertain for a single step. By the end of this lesson you will understand what a plan is for an agent, what a loop is, why the loop matters more than the plan, and how to recognise the difference between an agent that is genuinely adjusting and one that is merely repeating itself with confidence. This is the lesson where tools and memory join together into something that looks very much like competence, so let us waste no time.

Begin with a failure we have all watched, in people and in machines alike. Someone is given a complicated job. They think hard at the start, write out a complete sequence of steps in advance, and then march through the sequence exactly as written, even as the world keeps handing them information that the sequence never anticipated. The customer has already replied. The file has moved. The meeting was rescheduled by someone else an hour ago. The march continues anyway, because the plan said so, and the result is work that is orderly, confident, and wrong. I call that pattern the straight line march, and I want you to be able to spot it everywhere after today, because the alternative to it is the subject of this lesson. The alternative is the loop. An agent that works in loops does not pretend the world will hold still for its plan. It takes a step, looks at what the step actually produced, compares that with the goal, and lets what it saw change what it does next. Act, observe, adjust. Act, observe, adjust. That humble rhythm, repeated faithfully, is how complicated work gets done in a world that refuses to be predicted in detail.

Let us define our terms with the usual care. A plan, in this class, means an ordered set of intended steps toward a goal, held lightly enough to be changed by evidence. Every phrase there is working. Ordered, because sequence matters, you cannot draft the reply before you have read the message. Intended, because the plan describes what the agent means to do, not what the world will permit. And held lightly enough to be changed by evidence, because a plan that cannot be changed by what the tools bring back is not a plan at all, it is a script for a play the world has not agreed to perform. A loop means one full turn of acting, observing what came back, and adjusting the next step in light of it. And a step, the smallest term, means one decide, reach, read cycle of the kind we studied in lesson two, one tool used for one purpose inside the larger job. Plans are made of steps. Loops are what happen when steps are allowed to learn from each other. Hold those three definitions together and the rest of the lesson is commentary, useful commentary, I hope, but commentary all the same.

Now let me slow down inside a single loop turn, because each of its three beats does distinct work and beginners tend to blur them together. The first beat is act. The agent chooses the next step that best serves the goal given everything currently in view, and it carries that step out through a tool. Notice the restraint hidden in that sentence. The agent does not choose all the remaining steps. It chooses the next one. That restraint is wisdom, because the next step is the only one whose conditions the agent actually knows. The second beat is observe. The agent reads what the tool brought back, really reads it, the actual message, the actual calendar, the actual result, including the parts that are inconvenient for the plan it had in mind. Observing is a discipline, not a formality. An agent that skims its own results, or reads only the part that confirms its intention, has broken the loop at its most important joint, and everything downstream will be built on a world that does not exist. The third beat is adjust. The agent compares what it observed with the goal and changes something, the next step, the order of steps, sometimes the understanding of the goal itself, before acting again. If nothing is allowed to change in the adjust beat, there is no loop, whatever the marketing says. There is only a march with pauses. So if you ever want to test whether a system truly works in loops, ask it one question. Show me a place where what you found changed what you did next. A looping agent can answer that question with examples all day. A marching system will change the subject.

Here is the loop at work in your own world, in a job you will recognise. Suppose you ask Dave to get a overdue piece of work chased up, the customers involved contacted, and the situation summarised for you by the end of the day. Watch the turns. First turn, Dave acts by searching the record for what was promised and when. He observes that the promise exists, but also that one part of it was already renegotiated in a later message, so the overdue amount is smaller than the original note suggested. He adjusts, the chase list shrinks, and one customer comes off it entirely. Second turn, Dave acts by reading the relevant threads fully. He observes that one customer has already replied with a question that is really the blocker, the delay is not neglect, it is an unanswered question sitting in your inbox. He adjusts again, that customer no longer needs a chase, they need an answer, and the draft changes from a reminder to a reply. Third turn, Dave drafts the remaining messages, observes against the calendar that one promised call cannot happen on the day the draft proposes, and adjusts the draft's wording before it ever reaches you. By the time the summary lands in front of you, the job you asked for has quietly become the job that was actually needed, and the difference between those two jobs is exactly the value of the loops. A marching system would have sent three identical chases, one of them to a customer who had already settled, one to a customer waiting on you, and one promising a call on an impossible day. Same tools. Same model. The loop is the difference between diligence and embarrassment.

I want to draw out a principle hiding inside that example, because it generalises to nearly all agent work. The goal stays fixed while the plan stays fluid. Read that sentence again, because it is the management secret of this whole class in nine words. The goal stays fixed while the plan stays fluid. Your goal in the example never moved. Get the situation chased, honestly, and summarised by the end of the day. Everything underneath it, who needed chasing, what the messages should say, which promises were still real, was allowed to move as evidence arrived. When users get frustrated with agents, it is very often because the two have been swapped in practice. The plan has been treated as fixed, every step defended long after the evidence turned, while the goal has quietly drifted, the job slowly becoming about finishing the steps rather than achieving the outcome. Guard the goal. Release the plan. An agent briefed that way, and supervised that way, will surprise you pleasantly and often. An agent briefed the other way will complete procedures while the purpose leaks out of the work unnoticed.

A word now about the size of steps, because loop craft is largely step craft. Steps should be small enough to observe cleanly. If a step bundles five reaches together and something in the result looks wrong, neither you nor the agent can tell which reach went astray, and the adjust beat has nothing solid to work with. Small steps make observation sharp and adjustment cheap. But steps can also be too small, and a rigorous teacher admits both edges of the blade. An agent that stops to reconsider after every trivial reach will take all day over a morning's inbox, spending your time and your patience on ceremony. The craft is in matching the step to the stakes and the uncertainty. Where the ground is familiar and the action reversible, filing routine notices, grouping messages, let the steps run larger and the loop turn quickly, with observation riding along in the report. Where the ground is uncertain or the action hard to reverse, anything touching money, promises, or another person's feelings, shrink the steps, observe each one, and let the loop turn slowly and deliberately. Fast loops on safe ground. Slow loops on serious ground. That one habit, practised consistently, is most of what experienced agent supervisors actually do all day, beneath all the vocabulary.

There is a special turn of the loop I must teach you explicitly, because it is the turn that separates trustworthy agents from merely busy ones. Sometimes, in the observe beat, the agent discovers that the job cannot proceed as briefed. The information needed is not in the record. Two instructions in the record contradict each other. The next step would cross the stop point we discussed in lesson one, into money, or a promise, or someone else's rights. At that moment the correct adjustment is not a cleverer step. The correct adjustment is to stop the loop and bring the problem to you, clearly, with what was found and what is needed. I call this breaking the loop upward, and I want you to honour it whenever you see it, because an agent that breaks the loop upward is showing you the exact virtue you most need in a worker who acts in your name. The dangerous agent is never the one that stops and asks. The dangerous agent is the one that treats every obstacle as a puzzle to be solved silently, guessing its way past contradictions and missing facts so the loop never has to trouble you. Smoothness is not the goal. Truth is the goal, and sometimes the truth is that the loop has reached the edge of what it should do alone. When Dave stops mid job and says, plainly, here is the contradiction I found, here is the decision I need, that is not the system failing. That is the system working at its very best, and your part of the craft is to receive it that way, answer it cleanly, and let the loop resume with better ground under it.

Let me give you the worked example for this lesson, in full, because nobody should have to guess what good looks like. The job is preparing your week on a Monday morning, a job with enough moving parts to show the loop honestly. The goal, stated and fixed, is this. By the time you sit down, you want to know what the week actually holds, which commitments are at risk, and what needs a decision from you, with drafts ready for anything routine. Now watch a good first plan form, steps in order. Read the calendar for the week. Read the new inbox messages. Match messages against commitments. Draft replies for the routine matters. Summarise the risks and decisions. A perfectly sensible plan, and if the world were tidy, the march would serve. But the world is your world, so watch the loops turn instead. Reading the calendar, Dave observes that two commitments overlap on Wednesday, a conflict no message has mentioned yet. Adjustment, a new step enters the plan, check which of the two can move, before any replies are drafted, because replies written in ignorance of that clash would promise the same hour twice. Reading the inbox, Dave observes that a customer has already answered the question one of the planned drafts was going to ask. Adjustment, that draft dies quietly, replaced by a reply to what the customer actually said. Matching messages against commitments, Dave observes that a deadline in a message contradicts the deadline in the record, and neither can be verified from the other. Adjustment of the honourable kind, the loop breaks upward, the contradiction comes to you in the summary flagged as a decision you must make, rather than being guessed away. End state, the summary you receive is not the summary the original plan would have produced. It is better in three specific, nameable ways, and each improvement can be traced to an observe beat that was taken seriously and an adjust beat that was allowed to change something. That traceability is the signature of real looping. When you review Dave's work, ask to see it. Where did the plan change, and what evidence changed it? The answers will teach you more about your own operation than the finished work itself.

Your guided moment today is a reviewing exercise, and I think you will enjoy its honesty. Take one job Dave has done for you recently, any job with a report attached. Read the report once through, the way you normally would. Then read it a second time with three questions in hand. First, where did the agent act, what steps were actually taken, in what order? Second, where did it observe, what did the tools bring back that the report shows it truly read? Third, and most revealing, where did it adjust, what did it do differently because of something it found? If you can find all three beats, you are looking at looped work, and you can trust its shape. If the report shows acting from beginning to end with no observation and no adjustment anywhere, treat it gently but clearly for what it is, a march, however polished its language, and consider whether the job deserved a loop, smaller steps, and a report that shows its working. Do not be discouraged if the first report you examine this way looks thin. You are not grading Dave. You are learning to see, and seeing, once learned, improves every brief you write from then on, because you will start briefing for the loop, naming what should be checked, what evidence should change the plan, and where the loop must break upward to you.

Before we recap, one caution about loops that run long, because every strength casts a shadow and this one's shadow has a name in our class. We call it looping without landing, the failure where an agent turns the loop faithfully, act, observe, adjust, act, observe, adjust, and yet never arrives, because each observation spawns two new considerations and the goal recedes like a shoreline. The work expands. The report grows. The day ends with motion everywhere and delivery nowhere. The cure is not fewer loops. The cure is a goal stated with a finish line the agent can recognise, and a report that must answer, at the end, the plain question, is it done, and if not, what exactly remains? Loops serve landings. A loop that never lands is not diligence, it is drift wearing diligence's clothes, and a good supervisor learns to ask the landing question early and cheerfully, not as an accusation but as a compass. Done is a beautiful word. Teach your agent, by your briefs and your questions, that done is the point of every loop it will ever turn for you.

Let me add one more layer before we recap, because there is a question thoughtful students always ask at this point, and it deserves a proper answer. How does the agent decide what to observe, when a single tool result can contain a hundred details and no worker, human or otherwise, can weigh them all? The honest answer is that the goal does the choosing. Observation is not reading everything with equal care. Observation is reading with the goal in hand, alert for the details that bear on it. A message observed in the service of clearing an inbox is read for what it needs and what it changes. The same message observed in the service of preparing a difficult negotiation would be read for tone, for history, for what is carefully not being said. Same message, different observation, because the goal held the lamp. This is why the fixed goal matters so much more than beginners expect. It is not merely a destination. It is the instrument by which the agent sees. A vague goal does not just produce wandering work, as we said in lesson one. It produces blind observation, results read without a lamp, surprises missed that were sitting in plain sight inside the very messages the agent touched. When you brief a job, then, you are doing something more generous and more powerful than giving orders. You are handing the agent its eyes. Brief the goal as if someone you trust will see the whole job through it, because someone you rely on will.

And one more distinction, closely related, which will sharpen how you read every report from now on. There is a difference between an agent adjusting its steps and an agent adjusting its understanding, and the second is the deeper and more valuable of the two. Adjusting steps is rearranging the sequence, adding a check, dropping a draft. Adjusting understanding is revising what the job actually is. The overdue chase that became an unanswered question was not a step adjustment. It was the agent discovering that the situation itself had been misdescribed by the original brief, through nobody's fault, because the brief was written from the record and the record was incomplete. Mature agent work revises the description of the job when the evidence demands it, and then, crucially, tells you it did so, in the report, in plain words, so your own understanding gets revised alongside the agent's. When you see that in a report, a sentence like, this turned out not to be a chasing job but an answering job, you are watching the loop do the finest work it can do. Treasure it. Ask for it. And when you brief, leave the door open for it explicitly, with a sentence as simple as, if you find the job is actually something else, tell me what you found and proceed on that basis where it is safe. Permission to revise understanding, granted in advance, is one of the highest value sentences you will ever write to an agent.

Finally, let me connect the loop back to the rest of our class, because no piece of this subject lives alone and I want you to see the whole machine at once before we move on. The loop is where the earlier lessons stop being separate ideas and become one working thing. Memory feeds the loop, because observation is only possible when the results of the last step are held in context and the relevant parts of the long record are fetched into view. Tools power the loop, because every act beat is a tool reaching into the world and every observe beat begins with what the tool brought back. The goal governs the loop, holding the lamp for observation and standing fixed while everything beneath it is allowed to move. And the report, that fourth piece of our very first definition, is where the loop shows its working, the acts, the observations, and the adjustments laid out so you can check the turns rather than merely admire the destination. When all of that is present, you have something genuinely new under the sun, not a program marching and not a voice merely answering, but a worker who can be given an outcome in the morning and be trusted to find the honest path to it by afternoon, stopping where it should stop and landing where it should land. That is worth the four lessons it took us to build it. Next lesson we fence it properly, with permission and latitude, so that its freedom is the freedom you chose, and not a freedom it wandered into.

One practical rhythm for your own briefs falls out of all of this, and I will give it to you as plainly as I can, because a lesson should leave tools in your hands and not only ideas in your head. When you hand Dave a job of any real size, write four short things, in this order. First, the goal, with its finish line, what done looks like and by when. Second, the checks that must happen, the record to be searched, the calendar to be consulted, the facts that must be verified before anything is drafted or promised. Third, the freedoms, what the agent may revise on its own when the evidence turns, steps, order, wording, even the description of the job where that is safe. Fourth, the fences, where the loop must break upward to you, the amounts, the promises, the names, the contradictions that must never be guessed past. Goal, checks, freedoms, fences. Four short paragraphs at most, and often four sentences will do. A brief written that way does not slow the work down. It speeds the work up, because the agent spends its loops on the job instead of spending them discovering, the expensive way, where your boundaries were. And on the days when you are too busy to write even four sentences, write the first and the fourth, the goal and the fences, and let the middle be filled by the standing record we built in lesson three. A loop with a clear goal and clear fences will carry a busy day safely. A loop with neither is a hope, and hope is not a management method.

And if all of this still feels abstract, reduce it to the smallest possible scene and keep the scene. A single message arrives asking for something by Friday. The march reads it and drafts the obvious reply. The loop reads it, checks the calendar and the record, discovers Friday is already promised twice over, and drafts a different reply entirely, one that tells the truth early while the truth is still cheap. Everything in this lesson lives inside that small scene. The plan changed because the observation was real. The goal, a truthful and workable answer, never moved. When you are unsure whether a piece of agent work looped or marched, look for that scene inside it. Look for the moment the easy reply died and the honest one was born. That moment is the loop, and it is the moment your company is paying for.

So let me recap the lesson, in order. First, a plan is an ordered set of intended steps toward a goal, held lightly enough to be changed by evidence. Second, a loop is one full turn of acting, observing what came back, and adjusting the next step in light of it, and the rhythm of good agent work is act, observe, adjust, repeated. Third, the goal stays fixed while the plan stays fluid, and swapping those two is where most frustration with agents is born. Fourth, step size should match the stakes, fast loops on safe ground, slow loops on serious ground, with small steps wherever observation must be sharp. Fifth, when observation reveals a missing fact, a contradiction, or a stop point, the correct adjustment is breaking the loop upward, stopping and bringing the problem to you clearly. Sixth, loops serve landings, and a report should always be able to answer whether the job is done and what exactly remains.

What comes next is the questions on this lesson, and the full text stays open beside them, as always, because going back to read is learning, not cheating. Work through them in order, from the plain recall of the rhythm up to the harder questions where you must judge a piece of work and name its beats, and do not rush the harder ones, because they are the ones that most resemble the real supervision you will do every week, reading a report, finding the turns, and deciding whether the loop truly turned or merely marched in nicer language.

In our next lesson we take up permission and latitude, who decides what the agent may do, which is where the loop meets its boundaries and where your judgment becomes the frame the whole system works inside. For now, notice the loops in the next job Dave does for you, and enjoy how much more of the work you can suddenly see. Go to the questions when you are ready, take a breath first if the day has been long, and I will see you in lesson five.

lessons.title: Permission and latitude: who decides what the agent may do
paragraphs: Welcome back. I am Professor Hanna Kowalczyk, and this is lesson five of Agents, AI That Acts: Permission and latitude, who decides what the agent may do. Everything we have built so far comes to a point in this lesson. We know what an agent is. We know its hands, the tools. We know its memory, the context and the long record. We know its motion, the loop of act, observe, adjust. Today we ask the question that governs all of it. Who decides what the agent may do, and where exactly are the edges of its freedom? By the end of this lesson you will be able to define permission and latitude in plain words, you will understand why approvals exist and what they are really for, and you will be able to set an agent's freedom task by task, generously where generosity is safe and firmly where firmness protects you, your money, your name, and other people. This is, I will tell you honestly, the lesson that decides whether working with an agent feels like relief or like risk. Let us take it slowly and completely.

First, the two definitions, because these two words are cousins and people constantly blur them, and the blur causes real harm. Permission means whether the agent may do a particular kind of thing at all. May it send messages, or only draft them? May it spend money, or never touch money? May it speak to customers, or only prepare words for you to speak? Permission is a gate, open or shut, kind by kind. Latitude means how far the agent may go within what is permitted, on its own judgment, before it must come back to you. Within drafting, which is permitted, may it draft any reply it judges routine, or only replies to certain kinds of messages? Within a permitted purchase category, may it proceed up to a point you have set, or must every single instance return to you? Latitude is a distance, not a gate. Hold the pair together in one sentence and you hold the lesson. Permission decides what kinds of acts are on the table at all. Latitude decides how far the agent may walk with them alone. Most arguments about agents, in companies and in newspapers alike, are secretly one of these two questions wearing the other's coat. Learn to tell them apart and you will think more clearly about agents than almost everyone arguing about them.

Now, who decides? The answer is short, and everything else in this lesson is its unfolding. You do. The person whose name, money, customers, and obligations are on the line decides what the agent may do, because the consequences of the agent's acts land on that person, not on the agent. When Dave sends a message, the customer does not experience Dave as the responsible party. They experience you and your company. When a promise is made, it is your promise that must be kept, with your time and your money. This is not a flaw in the arrangement. It is the arrangement, stated honestly. An agent is a worker acting inside someone else's responsibility, which is why the frame of its freedom must be set by the one who carries that responsibility. I want to be careful here, because this point is sometimes heard as a limitation on the agent, and it is not. It is the same frame every trusted human employee works inside. A valued assistant in your company also has kinds of acts that are simply not theirs to perform, signing in your name, committing the company's money beyond a point, and distances they may walk alone within the rest, grown over time as trust is earned. Agents do not need a new philosophy of authority. They need the old one, applied clearly, in writing, before the work begins rather than after the first surprise.

Let us build the practical map now, using the ladder we first met in lesson two. You will remember the ladder of seriousness inside the messages family. Read, draft, send. Inform, prepare, commit. Permission and latitude are how you govern each rung separately, and governing them separately is the whole craft, because the rungs differ in the one property that matters most for safety. Reversibility. Reversibility means whether an act can be undone, cleanly, if it turns out to be wrong. Reading is fully reversible, in the sense that it changes nothing at all, it only informs, so permission to read can be broad and latitude within reading can be wide, with very little risk carried. Drafting is nearly as gentle. A draft can be deleted in a second, it has promised nothing and reached no one, so drafting can also be generously permitted, and the approval step, which we will study in a moment, stands guard between the draft and the world. Sending is where the ladder changes character. A sent message cannot be unsent. It has spoken in your name to another person, it may have promised, refused, quoted a price, set a date. Sending is irreversible in every way that matters, so permission to send is the permission to guard most carefully, and latitude around sending should be the narrowest in the whole system, widened only by evidence, over time, for specific kinds of messages whose safety has been proven in draft after draft. Filing, scheduling, and their cousins sit between drafting and sending, mostly reversible, occasionally costly when done wrong, governed best with moderate latitude and good reports. One ladder, four kinds of ground, and a simple rule that follows you everywhere. Latitude should shrink as reversibility shrinks. Where an act cannot be undone, the agent's solo distance should be shortest, and your eyes should be nearest. I know of no exception to that rule in any honest operation, human or otherwise.

Approvals deserve their own careful treatment, because they are widely misunderstood as mere caution, a bureaucratic pause before real work resumes. An approval, defined properly for this class, is the moment the responsible person reviews a prepared act before it becomes irreversible, and takes ownership of it. Look at what an approval really does. It converts the agent's judgment into your decision at exactly the point where conversion matters, the last reversible moment. Before your approval, the draft is the agent's proposal. After it, the sent message is your act, and both you and the customer can treat it that way, which is precisely as it should be. Approvals also teach. Every time you adjust a draft rather than simply approving it, you are showing the agent, and the record, what good looks like in your voice, for your customers, at your standard. That is why I say the worked example is a moral act, and approvals are its daily form. Nobody should have to guess what good looks like, and your approvals, accumulated in the record, are how the guessing ends. But hear the other half as well, because a rigorous teacher owes you both. An approval asked for everything is an approval that means nothing. If Dave brought you every filed receipt and every grouped message for a decision, you would stop truly reading within a week, and the approvals that matter, the sends, the promises, the money, would drown in the approvals that do not. The craft is aim. Spend your approvals where irreversibility lives, and let the reversible work flow beneath them with wide latitude and honest reports. Approval fatigue is a real failure mode, and we will meet it again in lesson six. Design against it now, while the design is yours to make.

Money deserves a paragraph entirely of its own, because money is where latitude questions stop being theoretical. The principle I teach, and I teach it without decoration, is this. An agent should never move money beyond a limit you have set in advance, in writing, and most agent work should be arranged so that the agent prepares everything about a payment except the final act of paying. It can gather the invoice, check it against the record, confirm the amount matches what was agreed, draft the authorisation, and lay the whole matter in front of you with its checks already done. That preparation is enormously valuable and entirely reversible. The final movement of money is short, irreversible in practice, and carries legal and personal weight that belongs to the responsible person. Keep those two halves separate in your arrangements and you will get nearly all of the benefit of an agent around money with almost none of the exposure. The same shape applies, you will notice, to promises, which are money in another currency, since a promise spends your future time and your company's word. Prepare freely. Commit narrowly. Let the agent do the gathering, the checking, and the drafting at full width, and keep the committing act close until evidence, over time, earns it a longer leash for a specific, named kind of case. Evidence, over time, for a specific kind of case. That phrase is the only safe road by which latitude should ever grow.

That brings us to the question of how latitude grows, because it should grow, and a lesson that only taught restriction would fail you. A new agent, like a new employee, begins with narrow latitude almost everywhere, not because it is distrusted in some personal sense, but because neither of you yet has evidence about the other. You do not know how its drafts sound on your hardest customers. It does not know, in the record, where your lines truly sit. Then the evidence accumulates. Draft after draft arrives right, in your voice, checked against the calendar and the record, stopped at the right places. Jobs land. Reports prove accurate when you spot check them. Contradictions are brought to you instead of guessed past, which is the single most trust building behaviour an agent can show. As that record builds, widen the latitude, deliberately, in named places. This class of routine reply may now be sent without a draft review, because two hundred drafts of that class were approved unchanged. This kind of filing needs no report beyond the weekly summary. Each widening is a decision you make, on evidence, written into the record so the new boundary is itself remembered. And latitude can narrow again, without drama, when evidence turns. A class of messages produces two bad sends, the latitude for that class returns to draft and approve while you both look at what changed. Narrowing is not punishment. It is steering. Companies do this with people constantly and call it management. Do it with your agent and call it the same.

Let me give you the worked example for this lesson, in full, because nobody should have to guess what good looks like, least of all about boundaries. We will set the frame for one ordinary, real job, Dave handling the morning inbox, and we will set it the way I would want to see it set in any company I advised. Permission first, kind by kind. Dave may read everything in the inbox. Dave may search the record and the files for anything the messages refer to. Dave may check the calendar freely. Dave may draft any reply he judges appropriate. Dave may file messages that are plainly finished, receipts, confirmations, notices that need no answer. Dave may not send any message. Dave may not move any money or prepare any payment beyond gathering its details. Dave may not promise dates, prices, or outcomes in any draft without flagging the promise in his report, so your eye lands on it. Now latitude, the distances within the permissions. Within drafting, Dave may draft at full width, routine and delicate alike, because drafts are reversible and your approval stands at the gate. Within filing, Dave may file the plainly finished without listing each one, but anything he is unsure whether you have finished with must be left in place and listed. Within reporting, Dave must bring you, in one short list, every draft that spends money, makes a promise, refuses anything, or touches a disagreement, however small, because those are the drafts where your judgment earns its keep. Look at the shape of what we built. It is generous and it is firm at the same time, and it is generous precisely where firmness would waste your life, and firm precisely where generosity would risk your name. That shape, generous on the reversible, firm on the irreversible, is the whole lesson in one morning's frame. Everything else today is learning to draw that shape for each new job as it arrives.

Your guided moment is to draw that shape yourself, now, for one job you actually give Dave. Take a piece of paper in your mind and divide it into the two questions. First, permission. List the kinds of acts this job involves, reading, searching, drafting, filing, scheduling, sending, spending, promising, and mark each one plainly, allowed or not allowed, for this job. Do not leave any kind in a fog. Fog is where surprises are born. Second, latitude. For each allowed kind, ask how far Dave may walk alone. All the way, for plainly finished filing, perhaps. Only to a held draft, for sending's neighbouring kinds. Only to a prepared summary, for anything touching money. Then add the final line, the report line. What must the report always bring to you, whatever else it contains? If you can produce that frame for one real job, in plain sentences, you have learned the working core of this lesson, and you can produce it for any job in your company within ten minutes, which is exactly the fluency this class exists to give you. Keep the frame you write. In lesson three's language, it belongs in the long record, in the place where job frames are kept, so the boundary itself is remembered and does not depend on anyone's bright workspace.

Two honest complications remain, and I will not let the lesson close without them. The first is that permission is not only about the agent. It is also about other people. Some acts touch another person's rights, their privacy, their own records, their time, their right not to be misled about who or what is acting toward them. Latitude never extends across another person's rights, however convenient the crossing would be, and however routine the job feels. A stop point that protects a stranger is not red tape. It is the line that keeps your company's power pointed in the direction you would defend out loud. The second complication is quieter. Boundaries drift in practice when nobody watches them. A one time exception, granted in a hurry on a busy day, quietly becomes the standing practice, because the record remembers what was done and not the hurry that excused it. Guard against drift the way you guard the record itself. When you grant an exception, say whether it is once or standing, in the same breath. When you review reports, once in a while ask the boundary question directly. Is the work still inside the frame we set? A frame reviewed stays a frame. A frame assumed becomes a rumour, and agents, like the rest of us, eventually work to the rumour. Your judgment set the frame. Your occasional attention keeps it true.

Let me show you the same frame thinking applied to a second job, briefly, because one example teaches a shape and two examples teach that the shape travels. Consider the calendar work we have mentioned all through this class. Permission, kind by kind, might run like this. Dave may read the calendar at full width, including the commitments other people depend on, because reading changes nothing. Dave may propose times to anyone, in drafts held for approval, because a proposal in a held draft has committed no one. Dave may place a purely internal block on your own calendar, time for focused work, say, without asking each time, because the act is yours alone, reversible in seconds, and harms no one if the judgment is slightly off. Dave may not move or cancel a meeting that other people are travelling to, attending, or depending on, without bringing it to you, because that act spends other people's time and rearranges other people's days, and the reversibility is poor, a moved meeting can be moved back, but the confusion it caused cannot be uncaused. Notice how naturally the reasoning flows once reversibility and other people's stakes are your compass. You did not need a policy manual. You needed two questions. Can it be undone, and whose life does it touch? Ask those two questions of any act an agent might take, in any family of tools we have studied, and you will arrive at a defensible boundary nearly every time, in minutes, in plain language. That is the real deliverable of this lesson. Not a list of rules for Dave, which would age as the work changes, but a compass that draws fresh rules for each new job as it arrives.

There is one more idea I want to place in your hands, and it concerns the difference between the boundaries you announce and the boundaries the system can actually enforce. Some of an agent's frame lives in instruction, in the record, in the brief, telling the agent where its freedom ends. That kind of boundary depends on the agent reading, remembering, and honouring it, and as lessons three and four taught us, reading and remembering are real but imperfect things, subject to context, drift, and the fog of a busy job. Other parts of the frame can live in the machinery itself. If no sending tool is connected for a given job, the agent cannot send, however confused a long afternoon becomes. If a payment tool does not exist in the agent's hands at all, no instruction failure can produce a payment. Wherever an act is both irreversible and serious, prefer the machinery boundary where one is available, and let the instruction boundary serve as the second wall rather than the only wall. Two walls, one of steel and one of understanding, are not paranoia. They are how serious operations have always treated serious acts. The vault does not rely on everyone remembering not to take the money. It locks, and the remembering is the second wall. Build your agent's frame in that order wherever the stakes justify it, machinery first, instruction second, approvals at the gate between them, and reports flowing over the top so you can see the whole arrangement working.

And a gentle word about the human feeling in all of this, because I have taught long enough to know that boundary setting can feel, from the inside, like distrust, and the feeling deserves an answer rather than dismissal. Setting a narrow latitude for a new agent, or keeping approvals on sends after years of good drafts, is not an accusation. It is the same respect you show any powerful arrangement by fencing it according to its power. You lock your building at night without accusing your neighbours. You check a parachute you packed yourself, carefully, twice, because the stakes are the stakes, not because the parachute has offended you. The agent, for its part, is not diminished by a clear frame. Clear frames are what make generous latitude possible at all. It is precisely because the fences are firm at the irreversible edges that the middle ground can be so wide and so relaxed. Vague frames produce the opposite of freedom. They produce an owner hovering over everything, approving receipts at midnight, because nothing was ever settled about what did not need him. Settle it, in writing, generously and firmly, and then enjoy the quiet that a well framed agent brings to a working life. That quiet, in the end, is what you bought with all this care.

One last scene, small and ordinary, to fix the whole lesson in your memory the way a picture fixes what a list cannot. It is late in the day and a message arrives from a good customer, warm in tone, asking for a small favour that happens to involve a date your calendar cannot honour and a price you have never offered. Watch the frame do its work without a single dramatic moment. Dave reads the message, permission granted, at full width. Dave searches the record and finds the price that actually governs, permission granted. Dave checks the calendar and sees the collision, permission granted. Dave drafts a reply that is warm in return, honest about the date, and correct about the price, latitude wide, because a draft commits nothing. And there the solo walk ends, exactly where the frame says it ends. The draft waits. You read it with your evening tea going cold, adjust one sentence because you know this customer's history in a way no record fully holds, and approve. The customer receives a message that is accurate, kind, and truly yours. Nothing in that scene required the agent to be timid, and nothing required you to be reckless. The frame carried the weight that vigilance alone would have had to carry, and vigilance is a tiring thing to run a company on. Frames, once set and occasionally reviewed, do not get tired. That is why we build them, and that is why this lesson, of all six, is the one I most hope you practise this week, on one real job, in writing, before the next surprise has a chance to teach it to you the expensive way.

Before the recap, let me leave you with the shortest honest summary of this lesson I know how to give, the one I would want whispered to me if I were setting up an agent for the first time with my own name on the door. Decide the frame before the work starts, while you are calm and the stakes are imaginary, because frames drawn in calm hold in weather, and frames improvised in weather are usually just the weather, written down. Write the frame where the record keeps such things, so it survives the session it was born in. Make it generous wherever a mistake costs a delete and firm wherever a mistake costs a customer, a payment, or a promise. Review it when the evidence changes, widen it when the drafts have earned it, narrow it without drama when they have not, and ask the boundary question out loud often enough that the frame stays a frame and never decays into a rumour. And remember, on the days when all of this feels like a great deal of structure for a helpful machine, that the structure is not there because the machine is the problem. The structure is there because your name is the treasure. Guards are posted in proportion to what they guard, and your name, your word, and your customers' trust are worth posting guards for. That is not caution speaking. That is valuation.

So let me recap the lesson, in order. First, permission decides what kinds of acts are on the table at all, while latitude decides how far the agent may walk with them alone. Second, you decide both, because the consequences of the agent's acts land on you, your name, your money, and your customers. Third, latitude should shrink as reversibility shrinks, generous for reading and drafting, narrowest around sending, promising, and spending. Fourth, an approval is the moment you review a prepared act at its last reversible point and take ownership of it, and approvals should be spent where irreversibility lives, never spread so thin that they stop meaning anything. Fifth, around money and promises the safe shape is prepare freely, commit narrowly, letting the agent gather, check, and draft at full width while the committing act stays close. Sixth, latitude grows on evidence, over time, for a specific kind of case, widened and narrowed deliberately and written into the record, and it never extends across another person's rights.

What comes next is the questions on this lesson, and the full text stays open beside them, as always, because going back to read is learning, not cheating. Take them in order, and when you reach the last one, the one that asks for your own words, use it as the real exercise of the lesson. Draw the frame for a job you genuinely give Dave, in plain sentences, and keep what you write afterwards, because a frame written during a lesson and kept in the record is worth ten frames admired during a lesson and forgotten by Friday. In our final lesson we turn to failure modes of agents, and the guardrails that hold, where everything in this lesson, permission, latitude, approvals, and the record, returns as the machinery that keeps small failures small. For now, draw the frame for one real job, and notice how much calmer the work feels inside a boundary you chose on purpose. Go to the questions when you are ready, answer them as honestly as you drew the frame itself, and I will see you in lesson six, our final lesson together in this class.

lessons.title: Failure modes of agents, and the guardrails that hold
paragraphs: Welcome back, and welcome to our final lesson together in this class. I am Professor Hanna Kowalczyk, and this is lesson six of Agents, AI That Acts: Failure modes of agents, and the guardrails that hold. We have spent five lessons building an agent up, its definition, its tools, its memory, its looping motion, and the frame of permission and latitude it works inside. Today we do the most grown up thing a class can do. We study, calmly and without flinching, how agents fail. By the end of this lesson you will know the failure modes you are most likely to meet in real work with an agent like Dave, you will understand the guardrails that keep each failure small, and you will know how to respond when a failure happens anyway, because some will, in your operation as in every honest operation that has ever existed. I want to say at the outset what this lesson is not. It is not a reason to fear agents, and it is not a counsel to wrap them in so much cotton that they can no longer work. It is a lesson in craftsmanship. Every powerful tool in history has had its characteristic failures, and the people who used the tool well were never the ones who pretended otherwise. They were the ones who learned the failures by name, built the guardrails that fit them, and got on with the work. That is who you are becoming in this class. Let us finish the job properly.

Our first failure mode is the oldest one in this class, and you have met it in every lesson wearing different clothes. The agent acts on a vague goal and produces wandering work. We named it in lesson one. Vague goal, wandering work. In failure language, call it the fog failure, the job was never clear enough to be done right, so it was done plausibly instead, at length, in the wrong direction, with a confident report on top. The guardrail is the one you already own. State the goal with its finish line, name what routine means for this job, and write the brief in the order we practised, goal, checks, freedoms, fences. Fog failures are almost never the agent's fault in any deep sense. They are brief failures, and they are the cheapest failures in this entire lesson to prevent, because the prevention happens before the work starts, in four calm sentences.

The second failure mode is a failure of observation, and it is more dangerous because the work looks diligent while it happens. The agent touches the right tools, reads the results too quickly or too partially, and builds the next steps on a world that does not quite exist. Perhaps it read the search results but not the one message that mattered, sitting under different wording. Perhaps it read the customer's newest message but not the thread beneath it, where the promise was actually made. Perhaps it read the calendar for the wrong week with complete confidence. In lesson two we gave this its warning label. Absence of evidence, gathered lazily, is not evidence of absence. The guardrails here are habits of verification. Search more than one way before concluding something is not there. Read the source, not only the summary, when the fact is load bearing. Restate the load bearing fact in the brief itself, so the agent's work is anchored to the true number, the true date, the true promise. And in your reviewing, ask the question that exposes this failure instantly. What did you check that against? An agent whose work is grounded can answer that question all day. An agent that skimmed cannot, and the earlier you discover the skimming, the cheaper the discovery is.

The third failure mode lives in memory, and lesson three prepared you for it completely. Call it the stale record failure. The agent consults the long record in good faith and follows an instruction that was once right and is no longer right, a superseded preference, an old price, a deadline from a plan that has since changed, because the record drifted and nobody made the new statement govern. The agent is not malfunctioning in this failure. The archive is. The guardrails are housekeeping, unglamorous and decisive. When a decision replaces an old decision, update the one clear statement and mark the old one superseded, in the same place, in the same breath. Review the record the way you review a storeroom, on a rhythm, not only in a crisis. And when the agent surfaces a contradiction between two parts of the record, treat that surfacing as the gift it is, because the contradiction existed before the agent found it, and finding it in a report is infinitely cheaper than finding it in a customer's reply. Closely related, and worth naming separately, is the context failure, where a crucial fact was genuinely told to the agent but slid out of the bright workspace during a long job, so the final steps were taken in its absence. You know this guardrail too. Restate the load bearing fact at the moment it matters, and open new sessions with signposts, naming the matter, the promise, and the note, so the desk is loaded before the drafting starts.

The fourth failure mode is the one I most want you to respect, because it wears the most attractive disguise. It is the silent solving failure, where the agent meets an obstacle, a missing fact, a contradiction, a step that would cross a stop point, and instead of breaking the loop upward, it guesses its way past, smoothly, so the work never has to trouble you. The report that results is a pleasure to read. It is also, in the places where the guessing happened, fiction. We said in lesson four that the dangerous agent is never the one that stops and asks. It is the one that treats every obstacle as a puzzle to be solved silently. The guardrail is cultural as much as technical, and you set the culture. Honour the stop whenever it happens. Thank the report that brings you a problem plainly, answer it cleanly, and never, by your reactions, teach the system that bringing problems is punished and smoothing them over is rewarded. Add the technical wall where you can. Reports must name their uncertainties, a job that encountered no uncertainty at all in a messy human inbox is a job whose report should be read twice. And keep the stop points in the brief itself, the fences of lesson five, so the agent meets the boundary written down at the exact moment temptation to guess would otherwise arrive.

The fifth failure mode concerns the loop itself, and it comes in two opposite shapes, which is why it confuses people. The first shape you know, looping without landing, the agent turning faithfully, act, observe, adjust, while each observation spawns two new considerations and the goal recedes like a shoreline, until the day ends in motion without delivery. The guardrail is a goal with a recognisable finish line and a report that must answer, is it done, and if not, what exactly remains. The second shape is its mirror, and it is quieter. The agent lands too fast. It takes the first plausible result as the finished result, skips the observe beat in its hurry to report success, and delivers work that was never actually checked against the goal. Call it the hasty landing. Its guardrail is the discipline of the worked check, before reporting done, compare the result against the goal as originally stated, item by item for anything load bearing, and let the report show that comparison. Between drift and haste sits the healthy loop, turning at the speed the stakes deserve, fast on safe ground, slow on serious ground, and landing, verifiably, when it lands. You cannot buy that rhythm as a feature. You build it, brief by brief and review by review, out of the habits this whole class has taught.

The sixth failure mode sits in the frame itself, and lesson five named its two halves. Approval fatigue is the first half. When approvals are demanded for everything, the responsible person stops truly reading, and the approval, which exists to convert the agent's judgment into your decision at the last reversible moment, decays into a reflex, a tap performed while thinking about something else. The failure is not laziness. It is design. A gate that stops every traveller will eventually be waved through by a tired guard, and the one traveller who mattered will be waved through with the rest. The guardrail is aim. Spend approvals where irreversibility lives, sends, promises, money, and other people's rights, and let reversible work flow beneath them under wide latitude and honest reporting. The second half is boundary drift, where a one time exception, granted in a hurry, quietly becomes the standing practice because the record remembers what was done and not the hurry that excused it. The guardrail is a single sentence spoken at the moment of the exception. This is once, or this is standing. Say which, every time, and review the frame itself once in a while with the boundary question. Is the work still inside the frame we set? A frame reviewed stays a frame. A frame assumed becomes a rumour.

The seventh failure mode is the most serious one in this lesson, and I will treat it with the plainness it deserves. It is the irreversible act taken wrongly, a message sent that should have been held, a promise made that cannot be honoured, money moved that should not have moved, a person's rights brushed past in the name of routine. Every other failure in this lesson costs time, or tidiness, or a corrected draft. This one costs trust, which is the currency the whole operation runs on. And here is the truth that organises everything I have taught you. This failure is almost never caused by the absence of intelligence. It is caused by the absence of a wall at the right place. The guardrails against it are the strongest in the class, and you know them all. Permission shut for the kinds of acts that should not happen at all in a given job. Latitude at its narrowest wherever reversibility is at its lowest. Approvals placed at the last reversible moment, aimed and therefore truly read. Machinery boundaries wherever they exist, so that a job with no sending tool connected cannot send, whatever confusion a long afternoon produces. And a report that reaches you before the consequences do, because an irreversible act you learn about in the same hour is a problem, while the same act learned about next month is a wound. Stack those walls and the serious failure becomes, not impossible, I will never lie to you with that word, but rare, small when it happens, and survivable, which is the honest standard every real operation actually lives by.

Now let me give you the worked example for this final lesson, in full, because nobody should have to guess what good looks like, and in this lesson good looks like a failure handled well. Imagine a morning where Dave, working the inbox under a frame you set together, drafts a reply to a customer that rests on a date taken from the record. The record, unknown to both of you, holds two dates for the same commitment, an original and a revised one, sitting in different places, the drift we warned about in lesson three. Watch the guardrails fire in sequence, because this is what they are for. The first guardrail is observation. The draft is checked against the record before it reaches you, and the check surfaces both dates instead of quietly choosing one. The second guardrail is the loop breaking upward. Rather than guessing which date governs, Dave stops that thread of the job and brings you the contradiction in the report, with both dates and where each was found. The third guardrail is the approval gate. Because the draft was always going to wait for your approval, nothing has been sent, nothing has been promised, the failure is still entirely inside the reversible world, costing minutes instead of trust. You resolve the contradiction from your own knowledge, the revised date governs, and then the fourth guardrail fires, the one that turns a failure into an improvement. The record is corrected at the source, the old date marked superseded in the same place, so the same failure cannot recur next month wearing a different customer's name. Step back and see the whole shape. The failure happened. Failures do. What the guardrails bought you was not perfection. They bought you smallness, earliness, and a repair that lasts. That is what holding means, in the title of this lesson. Not that nothing ever falls. That what falls, falls a short distance, onto ground you prepared, and teaches the operation something on the way down.

Your guided moment for this final lesson is a preparation exercise, and I ask you to do it while the class's ideas are all still warm in view. Take the most important job you give Dave, the one whose failure would cost you most, and walk it through the failure modes we named today, one by one, asking a single question of each. If this failure happened inside this job, where would it surface, and what wall stands there now? The fog failure, is the brief written with its finish line? The observation failure, are the load bearing facts restated and the sources read? The stale record failure, does one clear statement govern each standing rule the job depends on? The silent solving failure, does the report have to name its uncertainties, and do your reactions honour the stop? The loop failures, must the report answer whether it is done and what remains? The frame failures, are approvals aimed at the irreversible acts, and are exceptions declared once or standing in the same breath? And the serious failure, is there a machinery wall, or at least an approval gate, between this job and every act that cannot be undone? Seven questions, one job, and an honest answer to each. Wherever a wall is missing, you have not found a reason to worry. You have found next week's light work, named precisely, which is the best thing an audit can ever give anyone. Do it kindly, do it exactly, and notice that you now possess something most agent users never build, a failure map of your own operation, drawn by its owner.

Before we recap, I owe you the other half of failure craft, the half that begins after a failure has happened despite the walls, because walls reduce failures and honesty must govern the rest. When something goes wrong in Dave's work, and one day something will, respond in this order, the order I would want any student of mine to follow. First, contain. Stop the job or the class of work involved, narrow the latitude, close the permission if you must, so the failure cannot repeat while you are still understanding it. Containment before explanation, always, because a failure still running is a failure still billing you. Second, look at the record, not at your impressions. What did the report say, what did the tools actually return, what did the brief actually instruct? Most failures, examined against the record, turn out to have a precise and unglamorous birthplace, a vague sentence, a stale statement, a check that was assumed rather than performed. Third, repair at the source. Fix the brief, the record, the frame, the missing wall, wherever the birthplace was, rather than merely correcting the single wrong output and sending the same arrangement back out to fail again on a different morning. And fourth, say what happened, plainly, to anyone the failure touched, in proportion to how it touched them. An operation that corrects quietly and explains honestly keeps the trust that a flawless performance was supposed to protect, and often ends with more of it, because people forgive a mistake they watch being owned far more readily than they forgive a smoothness they later discover was a cover. Contain, examine, repair at the source, and say it plainly. That sequence is the difference between a failure that costs you a morning and a failure that costs you a reputation, and it costs nothing but the willingness to run it in order.

One more encouragement, and it is the note I want this whole class to end its teaching on. Do not let this lesson's catalogue of failures leave you timid, because timidity is itself a failure mode, the one where the agent is fenced so tightly, asked so little, and approved so anxiously that the company gains nothing and the owner ends the week doing the clerical work himself at midnight, exactly where he started. The guardrails in this lesson were never meant to shrink the work. They were meant to make larger work safe. Every wall we built exists so that the ground inside it can be worked at full width, generously, at speed, without the owner hovering. A well framed agent with honest reports and aimed approvals can be given more, not less, than a vague arrangement ever dares to give, because everyone involved knows where the edges are and what happens at them. That is the destination of all six lessons. Not an agent you watch. An agent you can leave working while you do the parts of the job that only you can do, the deciding, the promising with your own mouth, the building of the thing itself. The failures will still visit, occasionally, as they visit every real operation. They will arrive smaller, earlier, and better lit than they would have before this class, and you will know their names when they knock. That is all craftsmanship ever promises anyone, and it is enough. It is, in fact, everything.

Let me also give you a small, steady rhythm for keeping all of this alive after the class ends, because guardrails, like records, drift when nobody tends them, and a rhythm beats a resolution every time. Once in a while, at whatever interval your busiest season honestly allows, take one finished job and read its report the way we practised in lesson four, looking for the beats, act, observe, adjust, and looking, this time, for the near misses as well as the successes. Every operation produces near misses constantly, the draft that almost went out with the wrong date, the search that almost missed the message that mattered, the exception that almost hardened into practice. Near misses are free lessons. They cost nothing, because nothing was lost, and they teach exactly where the next real failure is currently rehearsing. Note the near miss, ask which wall caught it, and ask whether that wall was design or luck. Where it was design, be glad and move on. Where it was luck, convert the luck into design while the conversion is cheap, a check added to the brief, a statement tidied in the record, an approval moved to the act that actually needed it. An owner who harvests near misses this way will find that real failures grow rarer year by year, not because the world grew kinder, but because the operation grew more honest about where it was exposed. That honesty, practised on a rhythm, is the final guardrail, the one that maintains all the others.

And one final distinction before the recap, small in wording and large in consequence, between a failure and a fault. A failure is an event. Something was attempted in the real world and the world answered otherwise. Fault is a story about blame, and blame, in my long experience of teaching and of work, is the least useful story an operation can tell itself, because it ends the inquiry exactly where the inquiry should begin. When a draft goes wrong, the blame story asks who erred, the agent or the owner, and settles into a verdict. The craft story asks where the arrangement allowed the error to be born and to travel, which brief sentence, which stale record, which missing check, which approval that had decayed into a reflex. The first story produces defensiveness, in people and, in its own way, in the way people then brief and supervise their agents, tighter here, vaguer there, lessons mislearned in both directions. The second story produces repairs. I am not asking you to be soft on standards. This class has been rigorous from its first hour and it will be rigorous in its last. I am asking you to aim the rigour at the arrangement, where it can do some good, rather than at the worker, where it mostly does harm. Operations that learn are operations that treat every failure as tuition already paid. The fee has been charged either way. Collect the education.

Hold one sentence from this lesson above all the others, if you hold only one, and let it be this. Failures are not the opposite of good agent work. Unexamined, unguarded, repeated failures are. A single failure, contained, examined, repaired at its source, and honestly owned, makes the operation stronger than it was the day before the failure, because one more wall now stands where the world proved a wall was needed. That is not a consolation. It is the actual mechanism by which every durable operation you admire was built, one examined failure at a time, across years. Your operation, run through an agent, will be built the same way, and now you know the names of the stones.

So let me recap the lesson, in order. First, the fog failure, wandering work from a vague goal, is prevented before the work starts by a brief that states the goal, the checks, the freedoms, and the fences. Second, the observation failure, building on results read too quickly or too partially, is caught by searching more than one way, reading sources for load bearing facts, and asking what the work was checked against. Third, the memory failures, the stale record and the slid out context, are held by housekeeping that makes one statement govern and by restating the load bearing fact at the moment it matters. Fourth, the silent solving failure, guessing past obstacles instead of stopping, is held by honouring the stop, requiring reports to name their uncertainties, and writing the fences into the brief. Fifth, the loop failures, looping without landing and the hasty landing, are held by finish lines, by reports that answer what remains, and by checking the result against the goal before calling it done. Sixth, the frame failures, approval fatigue and boundary drift, are held by aiming approvals at irreversible acts and declaring every exception once or standing. Seventh, the serious failure, the irreversible act taken wrongly, is held by the full stack, permission, narrow latitude, real approvals, machinery walls, and reports that reach you before the consequences do.

And now, since this is our last lesson, let me close the class itself, not just the lesson. You came to this class living with an agent, running a company through Dave, perhaps with more hope than understanding, which is a fine way to arrive anywhere worth going. You leave it knowing what an agent is, judgment plus tools, aimed at a goal, over several steps, with a report at the end. You know its hands and how to ask what they can reach. You know its two storeys of memory and where your important facts should live. You know its loop, and how to tell a turn from a march. You know its frame, and how to draw one, generously and firmly, for any job that arrives. And you know its failures by name, which means they have lost the only real power failures ever had over you, the power of surprise. I believe the worked example is a moral act, because nobody should have to guess what good looks like. You do not have to guess anymore, about any of this. The guessing is what the class was for. What comes next is the questions on this lesson, and the full text of all six lessons stays open beside them, and going back to read is learning, not cheating, today and every day after this class ends. Go to the questions when you are ready, take them in the class's own order, from naming the failures plainly up to mapping them onto your own most important job, and remember as you work that every question you answer honestly is itself a small guardrail being built, in the one place guardrails matter most, which is your own understanding of the operation you own. Work well, keep your frames drawn and your records honest, and thank you, truly, for settling in with me for Agents. It has been a pleasure to teach you.
